Johannesburg, 26 July 2016 - Three people have been injured after a roof collapsed at the Phumulani Mall in Tembisa, Gauteng. Ekurhuleni emergency service's William Ntladi said EMS personnel accounted for three people with minor injuries at this stage. Video: eNCA

• Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information. We will bring you updates as more information becomes available.

JOHANNESBURG – Three people have been injured after a roof collapsed at the Phumulani Mall in Tembisa, Gauteng.

Ekurhuleni emergency service's William Ntladi said EMS personnel accounted for three people with minor injuries at this stage.

“The roof at the mall has been blown off and most of the damage was caused by water that entered the mall. Many shops were affected and vehicles were damaged. Some vehicle were rolled over by the storm,” he said.

Ntladi said the unusual weather phenomenon happened at 15;40 and only lasted about 20 seconds.

Emergency services were on the scene and customers were being evacuated.

There have been several sightings of a tornado in the area.

The Tembisa hospital was also affected by the tornado.

“We can confirm that the [Tembisa] hospital was affected by the tornado this afternoon.

“Employees' vehicles were damaged and carports were also damaged,” said Gauteng health department spokesman, Steve Mabona.

Mabona added that trees were uprooted causing damage to three ambulances.

“No person or patients were injured. Parts of the hospital's roof were affected but there was no impact,” Mabona said.

Sources at OR Tambo International Airport indicated there had been no disruption to flight plans or services due to the adverse weather conditions..

Press Release:


Warning: Extreme Weather
Emergency services have been on high alert this week as extreme weather conditions have wreaked havoc across the country. KwaZulu-Natal has seen roads closed due to heavy snowfall and communities affected by widespread flooding. Meanwhile tornadoes have touched down in Gauteng and torn apart areas of Magaliesburg and Thembisa, injuring people and causing damage to a mall and hospital. Carte Blanche asks: What is driving this extreme winter weather system?


Script:


FINAL SCRIPT EXTREME WEATHER


VO: Just this last week, the country was hit by snowstorms, extreme hail, heavy rains and flooding claiming 5 lives in KZN and leaving thousands stranded.

TSHEPO: Because of the change of weather, climate change, global warming we see, lot of, lot of changes we see that are unusual in nature. INT1 M6 // the weather events will be more extreme INT1 M24

VO: Two Tornados hit Gauteng in a space of just two days.

This clip is from Magalisberg, 70km West of Johannesburg – it was recorded on Monday.

25 hours later a second tornado hit Tembisa, a township between Pretoria and Johannesburg.

It delivered scenes from what felt like a Hollywood movie and not the local news – the tornado ripped the roof off a local mall, wrecked at least 10 cars, flipped two trucks and left hundreds homeless.

LINK: Walking down just one street in section 10, Tembisa and the devastation becomes absolutely clear, concrete electricity poles were snapped in half, sheeting from some of the houses flung at least 10 meters into the trees, and shacks were just completely destroyed.

VO: Victor Mokoatedi was coming home from work, and missed the destruction by minutes.

DEVI: How did you feel when you saw your house?
VICTOR: You know, it’s a disaster,
DEVI: I didn’t realize it was so strong.
VICTOR: Look at the sheet – it was bending them like that – we don’t even have a roof. //

VO: Citizen journalists around the city captured the chaos on their phones as it happened - posting the clips for the world to see using social media.

Security guard, Onismus Chidi, was on his way to work when he took this video and posted it on Twitter.

OMISNUS: that thing it was moving like that, it was going round and going down.
DEVI: what were people saying around you?
ONISMUS: The people are just saying it’s snake, it’s a what-what – because they didn’t know a tornado.

VO: While small aircraft pilot Evan Baillie, knows storms, he was also amazed by what he was seeing.

EVAN: I saw the funnel basically come out of the cloud and hit ground and then saw the debris field spinning around, and realized it was a tornado

VO: But tornados in South Africa are not as uncommon as we think, says Tshepo Ngobeni from the SA Weather Service.

THSEPO: It’s not abnormal. The tornado is just part and parcel of severe weather events.

VO: But for eyewitnesses like Tienie Kruger – the experience was far from normal – he took this clip almost in the eye of the storm.

TIENIE: It was just loud, it sounded like speakers distorting or something.

VO: Driving the extreme weather this week was a low pressure system, that becomes 'cut-off', or severed, from the main planetary circulation and spins off independently.

Forecaster, Edwin Thema, explains the Cut-Off Low phenomenon.

EDWIN: There is a band – you get area of activities – in there you get convective storms developing.

VO: While Tornados are simply a by-product of severe thunderstorms – just like heavy rain, lightening and hail - the warning period for a tornado, is rarely more than half an hour.

As cold air drops and warm air rises – it eventually twists into a spiral and forms a funnel cloud.

While images of last weeks’ tornados have been widely distributed – it’s not the first time South Africa’s has been blasted by one of these.

- In 1948, 700 homes were wrecked and four lives lost in Roodepoort.
- 1999, 25 people were killed and around 500 others injured, leaving 95 % of residents homeless in Mount Ayliff, Eastern Cape.

This is Zastron in the Free State in 2010. In 2014, another one hit Vryheid in KwaZulu Natal.

TSHEPO: We do have more tornados than recorded, it’s just the difference is if tornado hit where it is populated, obvious, people know about it. INT1 M4

VO: EKURHULENI Emergency Services’ are not new to tornado events either. In 2011, a tornado tore through Duduza on the East Rand – claiming one life and injuring 160 people. William Ntladi was on the scene following both tornados.

WILLIAM: In the whole of Ekurhuleni we had a couple of them already, we know what is happening, what is expected of us to do, and we bring in our specialist rescue team. // miraculously… no one critically injured and no died from thing.

VO: Edwin was on duty as the tornado struck Tembisa.

DEVI: What was happening in this office?
EDWIN: Everyone was going up and down. We had a watch previous about severe thunderstorms but now they were starting to happen. At the this stage we were thinking here comes another storm.

VO: But the storm took a violent turn moving rapidly from target to target.

LINK: After ripping through zone 10 in Tembisa, it finally made a turn at Phumulani Mall, the mall has been closed until engineers are able to assess the structural damage.

WILLIAM The mall is basically totally destructed, the roof part of it, because it is basically blown off, a lot of debris in the passages, the windows of the shops are being broken down completely.

VO: Tienie Kruger works about 500 m from Phumulani Mall.

DEVI: And you could see debris flying inside?
TIENIE: It actually took these zinks and made it look like paper,
DEVI: The sheeting used for some of these house?
TIENIE: yes, it looked like paper in there.

VO: Victor says not only did the tornado flatten his home, he was even robbed of his possessions.

DEVI: And your belongings?
VICTOR: Don’t even say that, because my clothes went missing.
DEVI: Did people take it?
VICTOR: No, it got sucked up. And even the blankets.
DEVI: What the neighbours say to you
VICTOR: Once that thing is happening, once that thing strikes everyone is looking for a safe place to hide.

VO: But for many South Africans – tornados are an unknown weather phenomenon.

Angela Cromaty didn’t know what to do, when she spotted the Tembisa Tornado along the walls of the estate where she lives with her family.

ANGELA: …hid under slab…

VO: Tshepo says they were on the right track, but South Africans should make an effort to become weather smart.

TSHEPO: if you can observe it from a distance, try and look for a solid structure and make sure that you stay away from it’s path if possible. Best advice – look for a solid structure and avoid to be in an open area, and avoid to be in a hall
DEVI: There’s a vacuum
TSHEPO: Where there is a lot of vacuum.

VO: South Africans should brace themselves. Thanks to climate change and global warming - this is the new normal.

TSHEPO: It’s not unusual - extreme weather events will be with us from now onwards.

PROMOS

PROMO 1 – 10 seconds
VO: Two tornados, in two days blasted through parts of Gauteng.

WILLIAM: It’s a miracle that no one was critically injured or anyone died.

PROMO2 – 15 seconds
VO: A tornado ripped through Tembisa - blowing the roof off a local mall, wrecking at least 10 cars, flipping two trucks and leaving hundreds homeless.

VICTOR: Look at the sheet – it was bending them like that – we don’t even have a roof. //

PROMO3 – 15 seconds
VO: After snowstorms, hail and extreme flooding, South Africans were stunned when two tornados ripped through Gauteng.

THSEPO: The tornado is just part and parcel of severe weather events.

VO: Could this be the new normal weather pattern?
